recipes.title: Choose an editor for your programming workflow
recipes.description: Match graphical tooling, terminal habits, and licensing preferences. These are workflow choices based on documented features, not measured speed rankings.

picks.label: Broad graphical tooling
picks.reason: Integrated debugging, terminals, source control, and extensions support many languages in one workspace.
picks.tradeoff: The official Microsoft binary has different terms from the MIT-licensed Code-OSS source; extensions have their own licenses.

picks.label: Custom terminal workflow
picks.reason: Lua configuration and an embeddable API suit users who want to assemble a keyboard-driven environment.
picks.tradeoff: Modal editing and plugin configuration require learning and ongoing choices.

picks.label: Integrated terminal features
picks.reason: Multiple selections, Tree-sitter editing, and built-in LSP support provide a cohesive terminal editing model.
picks.tradeoff: Its selection-first controls differ from Vim and GUI editors.

picks.label: Paid text-editing focus
picks.reason: Multiple selections and project navigation suit intensive text manipulation in a graphical editor.
picks.tradeoff: Continued use requires a paid license, and deeper IDE features can require plugins.

recipes.title: Pick a Python workspace for learning or analysis
recipes.description: A debugger for learning, an interactive scientific IDE, and notebooks solve different problems.

picks.label: Learn program execution
picks.reason: Its teaching-focused debugger exposes expression evaluation and variable state.
picks.tradeoff: Larger multi-language projects may need a broader development environment.

picks.label: Inspect scientific variables
picks.reason: An IPython console and variable explorer support array and dataframe investigation beside scripts.
picks.tradeoff: Scientific dependencies and environment selection must be kept consistent.

picks.label: Combine code and explanation
picks.reason: Notebooks keep narrative, code, outputs, and data exploration together.
picks.tradeoff: Kernel and execution-order state need discipline for reproducible results.

recipes.title: Review changes and manage Git history
recipes.description: Choose by operating system and preference for a terminal, a guided client, or deeper graphical history tools.

picks.label: Terminal Git workflow
picks.reason: Status, diffs, staging, branches, and rebasing remain accessible from a keyboard-driven interface.
picks.tradeoff: The visual interface does not remove the need to understand history-changing operations.

picks.label: Guided commits
picks.reason: Visual diffs and a focused commit workflow help users review what they are about to commit.
picks.tradeoff: Official distributions support Windows and macOS; advanced Git actions may need the CLI.

picks.label: Windows repository inspection
picks.reason: A commit graph, branch tools, and Windows integration support detailed repository work.
picks.tradeoff: Windows prerequisites and Git configuration still need setup.

picks.label: Paid desktop history tools
picks.reason: Visual interactive rebase, image diffs, and a merge helper suit users who want a dedicated Git GUI.
picks.tradeoff: Windows/macOS only, with a paid license following evaluation.

recipes.title: Build API collections or inspect live HTTP behavior
recipes.description: Sending a request, maintaining a test collection, and intercepting application traffic are distinct tasks.

picks.label: Version API collections
picks.reason: Local plain-text collections can live with the application repository and be reviewed in Git.
picks.tradeoff: Some advanced and team features belong to paid editions.

picks.label: Standalone request CLI
picks.reason: Concise request syntax and formatted responses suit quick terminal investigation.
picks.tradeoff: Not every HTTPie option or behavior is implemented.

picks.label: Inspect and replay traffic
picks.reason: An intercepting proxy with scripting supports repeatable HTTP debugging of authorized targets.
picks.tradeoff: HTTPS interception requires explicit certificate trust and deliberate target configuration.

picks.label: Visual application interception
picks.reason: Application integrations and request filtering help inspect supported HTTP clients through a GUI.
picks.tradeoff: Advanced features and target integrations vary by plan and environment.

recipes.title: Inspect a local database or manage several engines
recipes.description: Start with the database engine and whether the task is browsing, querying, or administration.

picks.label: Local SQLite files
picks.reason: Visual tables and SQL execution let users inspect a SQLite file without a server.
picks.tradeoff: This is a SQLite-focused tool, not a multi-engine administration suite.

picks.label: Several database engines
picks.reason: Drivers, SQL editing, and data browsing share one cross-platform interface.
picks.tradeoff: Enterprise and cloud features can differ between Community and paid products.

picks.label: PostgreSQL administration
picks.reason: PostgreSQL-specific object and server tooling provides dedicated administrative context.
picks.tradeoff: It is specialized for PostgreSQL rather than every database engine.

picks.label: Integrated SQL development
picks.reason: Schema-aware SQL and interactive data tools suit database-centric development work.
picks.tradeoff: Free non-commercial eligibility and commercial subscriptions have different conditions.

recipes.title: Choose a local AI interface or inference runtime
recipes.description: Start with the model architecture and weight format, then check RAM or VRAM, the accelerator backend, and whether you need a desktop interface or an API. A file extension alone does not guarantee compatibility. No hardware benchmark or model-quality winner is claimed.

picks.label: Managed models and local API
picks.reason: Choose this for a managed local API or to import a compatible GGUF file or supported Safetensors model directory.
picks.tradeoff: Ollama does not quantize GGUF on import. Confirm your GPU and model support, memory budget, model license, and whether any cloud features are enabled.

picks.label: Detailed runtime control
picks.reason: Use this for direct GGUF loading with CPU or an available Metal, CUDA, or Vulkan backend.
picks.tradeoff: Check the model architecture and quantization plus the exact OS and backend build. Format or driver support is not a speed guarantee.

picks.label: Linux GPU Safetensors model serving
picks.reason: Choose this for an API server on a supported Linux GPU when the model architecture and Safetensors weights are supported.
picks.tradeoff: Check drivers, GPU support and VRAM, including room for the context cache. No native Windows support; GGUF is experimental and uses a separate plugin.

picks.label: Desktop chat interface
picks.reason: A graphical workspace offers local models alongside configured external providers.
picks.tradeoff: Privacy and cost depend on which provider and model are selected.

picks.label: Questions over documents
picks.reason: Document ingestion and retrieval can be organized into dedicated workspaces.
picks.tradeoff: A local installation can still send data to configured external embedding or model services.

recipes.title: Automate service flows or repetitive typing
recipes.description: Use a flow engine for events and integrations, and a desktop text expander for repeated text. These tools can be complementary.

picks.label: Event and device flows
picks.reason: Visual message flows and reusable nodes support service, API, and device integration.
picks.tradeoff: Installed nodes, credentials, and exposed endpoints require maintenance.

picks.label: Internal service workflows
picks.reason: Visual integration steps and custom code can be combined in hosted or self-hosted workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Its Sustainable Use and enterprise licenses are source-available, with restrictions beyond standard open-source licenses.

picks.label: Connector-based automation
picks.reason: Reusable pieces and visual flows support common service integrations.
picks.tradeoff: Community and enterprise portions use different licensing and features.

picks.label: Cross-application snippets
picks.reason: Typed triggers expand reusable text across supported desktop applications.
picks.tradeoff: Input permissions and application compatibility vary by operating system.

recipes.title: Choose tools for a modded game setup
recipes.description: Match the game and mod ecosystem before choosing a manager; an editor or conflict checker complements deployment rather than replacing it.

picks.label: Profiles and virtual files
picks.reason: Virtual-filesystem deployment separates managed mods from original files for supported games.
picks.tradeoff: Game support and a correct load order still need explicit verification.

picks.label: Nexus-centered workflows
picks.reason: Game extensions, deployment, and profiles integrate with supported Nexus Mods workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Extension support, filesystem requirements, and site account features vary.

picks.label: Isolated Minecraft instances
picks.reason: Separate instances organize Minecraft versions, loaders, Java settings, and modpacks.
picks.tradeoff: The game account and all selected Java, loader, and mod versions must be compatible.

picks.label: Bethesda record conflicts
picks.reason: Record-level views reveal plugin conflicts before creating a compatibility patch.
picks.tradeoff: This is a specialist editor; incorrect changes can damage a load order and require backups.

recipes.title: Choose an emulator for the console and title
recipes.description: Console coverage is the first filter. Then consult each project's game compatibility and setup documentation; game and firmware data are separate.

picks.label: GameCube and Wii
picks.reason: Controls and graphics configuration are specialized for GameCube and Wii software.
picks.tradeoff: Per-game compatibility and required controller behavior vary.

picks.label: PlayStation 2
picks.reason: PS2-specific configuration and rendering options support a large range of title-specific setups.
picks.tradeoff: A suitable BIOS and game data are required, and performance depends on the title and hardware.

picks.label: PlayStation 3
picks.reason: The project documents title compatibility and per-game configuration for PS3 emulation.
picks.tradeoff: Hardware demands are substantial for some titles; the official download page was blocked to this research environment.

picks.label: Unified multi-core frontend
picks.reason: A common interface shares controller and display configuration across compatible Libretro cores.
picks.tradeoff: Every core has separate compatibility and licensing; a frontend does not make all consoles equivalent.

recipes.title: Find the source of slow frames or expensive code
recipes.description: Match the measurement tool to the layer being investigated and use a reproducible workload.

picks.label: Rendering pipeline inspection
picks.reason: A captured frame exposes resource contents, shaders, and pipeline state for supported APIs.
picks.tradeoff: Use supported applications and APIs; upstream support is focused on programs you create.

picks.label: Instrumented native programs
picks.reason: CPU, memory, and synchronization events can be correlated on detailed timelines.
picks.tradeoff: Instrumentation needs integration and can influence the measured workload.

picks.label: Correlate system traces
picks.reason: Trace timelines and SQL analysis support multiple event sources in one investigation.
picks.tradeoff: System-wide recording is platform-specific; viewers and analysis tools have broader support.

picks.label: Inspect sampled stacks
picks.reason: Interactive profile views help examine expensive call paths in an imported profile.
picks.tradeoff: It is a viewer, so a separate profiler must first capture compatible data.

recipes.title: Choose a download tool for the transfer type
recipes.description: Select by protocol and automation needs, then use official sources and content you have permission to download.

picks.label: Automated resumable transfers
picks.reason: Several transfer protocols and an RPC interface suit scripted download queues.
picks.tradeoff: Remote-control interfaces need deliberate configuration and access protection.

picks.label: Desktop transfer queue
picks.reason: An aria2-based engine is exposed through a graphical queue.
picks.tradeoff: Site-specific logins or restrictions may need a different workflow.

picks.label: BitTorrent transfers
picks.reason: Desktop and optional web interfaces provide torrent management and transfer controls.
picks.tradeoff: Optional plugins and remote web access introduce additional configuration choices.

picks.label: Permitted media extraction
picks.reason: Site extractors, format selection, and FFmpeg integration support repeatable media workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Extractor compatibility changes with websites, and access rights remain separate from technical support.

recipes.title: Choose a browser by workflow and privacy needs
recipes.description: Browser engine, tab organization, defaults, and network routing are separate choices. No browser is claimed universally fastest or safest.

picks.label: Independent browser engine
picks.reason: Gecko and Firefox's extension ecosystem offer an alternative to Chromium-based products.
picks.tradeoff: Test required sites and extensions against the chosen browser and settings.

picks.label: Organize many web tasks
picks.reason: Tab workspaces, tiling, and panels support many concurrent websites in one interface.
picks.tradeoff: The full browser has proprietary terms and more configuration choices.

picks.label: Privacy-oriented defaults
picks.reason: A Firefox-derived configuration includes privacy settings and a content blocker.
picks.tradeoff: Stricter defaults and DRM choices can reduce compatibility with some sites.

picks.label: Tor routing and onion sites
picks.reason: The browser and Tor routing are configured together for a coordinated privacy workflow.
picks.tradeoff: Expect network and site-compatibility tradeoffs; extra plugins or identifying account use can undermine privacy.
